# Potential application of generative artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithm in oil and gas sector: Benefits and future prospects
Edward G. Ochieng a,* , Diana Ominde ^(b) , Tarila Zuofa ^(c)
- ^(a) *Professor of Project Management, Faculty of Business and Law, The British University in Dubai (BUiD), Dubai, United Arab Emirates* - ^(b) *Strathmore University, Strathmore Business School, Off Ole Sangale Road, Nairobi, Kenya* - ^(c) *University of Wisconsin-Parkside, College of Business, Economics, and Computing, Somers, WI USA, United States*

## *Keywords:*
Generative artificial intelligence Machine learning algorithm Value chain operations Oil and gas Productivity performance Risk management
#### ABSTRACT
With the rapid advancement of technology and societies, the global energy sector now acknowledges that by integrating contemporary digital technologies into their operations and capabilities, can improve their competitive advantage and innovation performance and processes. Moreover, energy operators are also facing a significant undertaking: how to best use and secure large amounts of data that promote sustainable productivity performance and minimise potential threats in the oil and gas value chain and project operations. In view of the foregoing, various facets like Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) and Machine Learning Algorithms (MLA) are increasingly gaining popularity within oil and gas sector operations. Thus, we explored how GAI and ML algorithms can enhance oil and gas value chain productivity performance. The Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was employed to identify significant GAI and MLA variables influencing performance in the oil and gas value chain, while Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was used to test regression equations related to their application. The study found that risk portfolios and profiles can be appraised throughout the value chain by effectively utilising GAI and ML algorithms in upstream, midstream and downstream undertakings. While these findings are noteworthy and have significant implications for current practice, the paper advocates that an array of digital technologies beyond GAI and ML can still be examined during future studies to demonstrate a holistic perspective on how digital transformation can be achieved across the energy sector value and project operations.
## **1.** **Introduction**
Energy generation and consumption are considered significant elements in national development, playing a vital role in a country's economic growth (Mombekova et al. [[1]](#page-12-0). As several existing energy fields approach their peak, the global need for energy resources is still increasing simultaneously. This continuously rising demand has led the oil and gas industry to move to more complex locations for oil and gas exploration and production operations resulting in several noteworthy implications and transformative moments for stakeholders. One of these includes balancing trade-offs in the quest for competitive advantage while expanding return on investments. Another is that the real-time monitoring of reservoirs and well operations now generates big datasets, necessitating highly efficient processing and analysis tools for decision-making regarding the oil and gas value chain [[2](#page-12-0)–4]. While AI is an advanced technology that enables machines to simulate human behaviour, ML (a subset of AI) leverages algorithms and models to learn
from past data or existing knowledge. As observed from the reviewed literature [[5]](#page-12-0), commercial corporations have discerned the potential of these applications in effectively enhancing their operations and realising their commercial objectives. In the energy sector, there has been a progressive adoption of various aspects of GAI and ML technology, a factor that continues to contribute to the growth of the sector [[6]](#page-12-0). Extant studies (see Ref. [[7]](#page-12-0); Li et al.*, *2021) affirmed that the energy industry is increasingly embracing emergent aspects of GAI and ML, a trend that has been noted to have contributed significantly to the expansion of the commercial space in the industry. The rise in the acceptance of these technological concepts in the energy industry has significantly improved their operations on various fronts ([[8](#page-12-0),[9](#page-12-0)]; [[10](#page-12-0)]; [[11]](#page-12-0)).
It is worth noting that the oil and gas industry faces a myriad of challenges in terms of its operational processes [[12](#page-12-0)]. Patel and Patwardhan [[13](#page-12-0)] suggested that operational inefficiencies both in the lower, mid and upper-stream operations continue to advance in complexity, necessitating the adoption of a new paradigm in terms of

In addressing the aim and research question, we adopted actionable research methods to ascertain the application of GAI and ML in enhancing productivity performance in the oil-gas value chain. Moreover, within the context of theoretical advancement we conceptualised and executed GAI and ML using preexisting sub-branches of the two. ## **2.** **Background**
#### *2.1.* *GAI and ML in the oil industry value chain*
The oil and gas industry and the core aspects of its value chain (upstream, midstream, downstream) remain critical for meeting global demand for fossil fuels, but they are also associated with unique risks and complexities that require innovative technological approaches. Broadly, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising technology for managing some of these complexities. GAI and ML algorithms are essential for advancing resilience, especially in varied and unpredictable environments like the oil industry value chain, by offering reliable and well-considered strategies.
The upstream sector comprises activities mainly related to mining, exploration, field development and production of crude oil. To achieve all these, the sector applies various ways of well-informed business decision-making processes that potentially increase production volume, reduce costs, boost safety, enhance operational performance, and safeguard the environment [21–[23]](#page-12-0). It is worth highlighting that most activities described above entail complex decision-making problems involving uncertainties while requiring significant input from wider industry stakeholders. The reviewed literature ([[21](#page-12-0),[22]](#page-12-0); Sheremetov et al.*, *2013) indicate the availability of a range of qualitative and quantitative decision-making support methods (DMS) to support stakeholders in the upstream sector. The application of these methods has led to an improved understanding of field and reservoir characteristics, how to embrace alternative production strategies like low carbon production technologies that ultimately drive more justifiable business decisions for brown and green field developments. According to Bratvold et. al [[24](#page-12-0)]. DMS can facilitate compliance with regulatory and risk management requirements while supporting the performance of technical and diagnostic tests of equipment. Common DMS methods used within the upstream sector include operational research methods such as linear programming, economic analysis methods, cost-benefit analysis, real options analysis, and environmental assessment methods. Even though Strantzali and Aravossis [[25](#page-12-0)] indicated that the single-criterion approaches have historically dominated decision-making in the upstream sector, the complexities and divergent interests involved in the decision-making process have equally resulted in the wider application of multi-criteria evaluation techniques. Such techniques can simultaneously consider multiple attributes involved in a decision-making problem like drilling technique or vessel selection, choice of appropriate maintenance strategies for different systems and components on oil and gas platforms, and determining the most viable decommissioning processes for facilities in the upstream sector. Nonetheless, to account for uncertainties associated with practitioners' subjective perception and experience, and several of the previously mentioned complexities, upstream operations are now gradually embedded with various forms of GAI and ML to augment the performance of the value chains. For instance, to improve recovery and extend economic viability, Chavan et al. [[26](#page-12-0)] acknowledged that enhanced oil recovery (EOR) is crucial for extracting significant volumes of hydrocarbons from declining reservoirs in existing and mature fields. Hence, they identified five machine learning algorithms to develop a standard data-driven EOR screening methodology. Of the five ML algorithms, the outcome of their study indicated that the random forest classifier exhibits the best prediction performance among the other classification methods.
Temirchev et al. [[27]](#page-12-0) developed an approach for predicting reservoir performance, which allows flow rate forecasting and managing dynamics of pressure and fluid saturations within reservoirs. Part of the outcomes of their study resulted in increased speed of reservoir modelling thereby attesting to how AI innovations have altered the upstream landscape. To further illustrate the rising popularity of GAI and ML in upstream operations, Sneed [[28]](#page-12-0) identified the key drivers behind electric submersible pump (ESP) failures (an expensive operational issue) and determined if it was possible to predict an ESP's
lifespan using predictive model techniques accurately. To achieve this, Sneed [[28](#page-12-0)] utilised ML applications to execute predictive maintenance on electric submersible pumps and select the ideal operational regimes relating to the production vs operational costs. Similarly, Hedge and Gray [[29](#page-12-0)] applied the use of ML to predict and increase the rate of penetration effectively. Their study aimed to guarantee the greatest contact between the productive piece of the development, the wellbore and the topmost pace of the construction of the well at negligible danger of failure. This resulted in a reduction of the nonprofitable time down to 20–50 % on average with a decline of approximately 90 % in failures with the growth and execution of ML. Koroteev and Tekic [[15]](#page-12-0), outlined three major opportunities for the application of GAI in reservoir engineering. The first relates to computations done with conventional reservoir modelling tools. The subsequent opportunity was linked to upscaling, which entails bringing the information gained from various scales of geophysical studies to a single geological and hydrodynamical reservoir model. The third opportunity akin to upscaling, involves using machine or deep learning to make history matching faster and less biased. In addition to applying GAI in reservoir engineering, they also demonstrated how it positively reduces the possible impact of catastrophes related to personnel health, safety and their operating environment.
Turning to the midstream sector, this sector principally focuses on the transportation of products (refined, semi and unrefined). As explained by Marchenko and Babyr [[30](#page-12-0)], the choice of transport mode for the transportation of products continues to pose a serious challenge throughout the production chain in the oil and gas industry. To address this issue, their study noted the importance of determining a rational route of delivery to justify the choice of a particular mode of transport while taking into account the timing of delivery products and cost considerations. Even though one current way of transporting petroleum products is via pipelines, Kraidi et al. [[31](#page-12-0)] observed that despite being popular, safe and economical, there are still concerns about safety and security in certain parts of the world with historically insecure environments and poor safety records. Therefore, to maintain a thriving midstream sector under the above conditions, there is a need to constantly adopt innovative technologies that can proactively respond to changing operational environments. However, due to inherent complexities, a common electronic integration of tools that support product supply, vessel distribution, pipeline scheduling, and storage might be insufficient due to the inherent complexities associated with the midstream sector. Rather, what is required is a unified approach to midstream sector optimisation using GAI and ML. Consequently, there are also many opportunities for applying GAI and ML in the midstream sector. In the U.S., Xiao et. al [[32](#page-12-0)]. recognised the crucial contribution of natural gas pipelines in meeting the ambitious climate goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. Consequently, they developed an efficient and reliable model to predict failures in gas transmission pipelines utilising historical failure data. Their model enhanced the accuracy of failure predictions for gas pipelines, offering valuable insights for improving safety and risk management practices.
Another area of interest for GAI and ML in the midstream sector is pipeline integrity management (PIM). According to Kishawy and Gabbar [[33]](#page-12-0), PIM encompasses pipeline inspection, testing, repair, assessment, and maintenance. While these activities are crucial for the integrity and life of the midstream sector infrastructure, they generate large datasets due to factors like pipeline length and the number of sensors and tools required to evaluate the pipeline and other infrastructure conditions. It is important to note that the generation of large datasets from PIM activities usually results in data management and processing challenges due to data volume, variety, and velocity. Potential implications of the above can result in complex manual analysis that can be time-consuming and error-laden. However, on a positive note*, *Xing et al. [[34]](#page-12-0) disclosed that ML could be applied to digest massive datasets and extract information and knowledge. Further studies by Loebbecke and Picot [[35](#page-12-0)] affirmed that ML algorithms can create lean pipeline integrity
management processes by augmenting productivity, providing autonomous information processing, and reducing reliance on manual and conventional data analysis.
With the rise in militant activity and rogue behaviour in some oil and gas regions around the world, Osegi (n.d.) proposed an AI predictive monitoring system capable of predictive classification and pattern recognition of pipeline datasets. Similarly, Eze et. al [[36](#page-12-0)]. developed an Integrated Oil Pipeline Monitoring and Incident Mitigation System (IOPMIMS), to effectively monitor and provide actionable information for pipelines by applying circulated frameworks and case-based thinking approach. Canelon et. al [[37](#page-12-0)]. presented a supervisory scheme based on multiagent systems as a methodology for the intelligent supervision of industrial processes with multiple feedback controls. One novel part of this administrative ML-optimised scheme was introducing a global supervisor agent with the capacity to establish mechanisms that guarantee the achievement of the global objectives of the entire industrial process. Sinha et al. [[38](#page-13-0)] utilised a multi-agent system as a core area of AI to deal with petroleum supply chain operations. When compared to conventional supply chain practices, the application of the multi-agent technology resulted in a faster supply chain. As part of their model, supply agents were led by supporting agents who arranged to enhance the predetermined subsystem cost, producing a less expensive inventory network. Julka et al. [[39]](#page-13-0) observed that refinery decision support systems (DSSs) do not integrate all the decision-making processes of refineries to interface with other systems that assist different departments simultaneously. Thus, they proposed a petroleum refinery integrated supply chain modeller and simulator (PRISMS), an agent-based framework for supply chain DSSs that emulates a refinery's supply chain and supports crude oil procurement. Compared to existing systems that use mathematical programming, the approach adopted by Julka et al.*, * *(*2002) was more versatile and straightforwardly captured the qualitative and transactional nature of the supply chain in the oil and gas industry.
The final sector of the oil and gas industry under examination is the downstream sector. This sector focuses on the process involved in the refining and conversion of oil and gas into finished products. Accounts by Patel et al.*, *(2020) indicated that the downstream sector is a complex, information-driven business with exponentially increasing volumes of information. In recent times, there has been a need for the sector to contend with capturing and monitoring more information and extracting useful data from available information. Their study also opined that advancements and innovations within this sector have resulted in reduced operational cost, improved quality of outputs and reduction in the negative impact on the environment [[40]](#page-13-0).
There are several other illustrations to depict the positive impact of GAI on performance in the downstream sector. Qing [[41](#page-13-0)] applied GAI in planning and scheduling, process unit optimisation, and preventive maintenance of equipment for downstream operations. Part of the study identified that the molecular-level advanced planning and scheduling systems can realise the cost performance measurement under different production schemes for diverse types of processable crude oil. Finally, since natural gas demand forecasting is one of the most crucial steps in the proper planning and operation of natural gas supply systems, Sharma et al. [[42](#page-13-0)] articulated the importance of balancing demand and supply of natural gas always. Thus, they developed a hybrid short-term natural gas forecasting model using various machine learning algorithms.
As scholars [[9,](#page-12-0)[43]](#page-13-0) noted, the digitalisation of all economic activities is occurring rapidly. So far, a cross-section of the studies examined from the reviewed literature indicates that this holds true for the oil and gas industry. For instance, Waqar et al.*, *(2023) noted that significant investments were made globally, including $52.9 billion by the U.S., $4.6 billion by the UK, and $17.2 billion by China, to enhance AI applications in various industrial sectors, including oil and gas. Specifically, Kuang et. al [[5](#page-12-0)]. observed that several global oil giants have now leveraged GAI to generate solutions for various stages of their design and production
activities. It can be concluded that GAI has several positive attributes in the oil industry value chain since it promotes product innovations, increases energy efficiency and supports improvements in hydrocarbon energy conversion. Finally, the US EIA [[44]](#page-13-0) report projected that global energy consumption will experience steady growth until 2050. From this projection, we believe that the use of GAI and ML will continuously increase in the oil and gas industry for the foreseeable future as there will be a need to embrace various technologies to develop existing and emerging fields. Despite these potentials, Tariq et. al [[45](#page-13-0)]. noted that there are several drawbacks associated with ML models. One challenge is the availability and accuracy of data used to build and test models. The data needs to be accurate in order to produce useful models. Thus, we assert that research on GAI and its application in enhancing productivity performance in the oil and gas value chain will remain a promising area. The next section is devoted to the research method, findings, discussion and conclusions.
## **3.** **Method and empirical setting**
The below section for the method has been divided into five parts.
- Data collection and sampling protocols - Principal component analysis - Structural equation modelling analysis - Manifest variables - General structural equation model hypothesised
## *3.1.* *Data collection and sampling protocols*
The data collection was conducted in three phases, namely: narrowing down determinants as identified during the literature review appraisal, developing questionnaire design, conducting a pilot study and administering the questionnaire survey. A three-phase piloting process was arranged: a draft copy of the questionnaire was given to two academics: one specialising in statistical analysis and another specialising in online questionnaire design. The other six experienced academics were knowledgeable in the field of project management, GAI, ML and oil and gas operations. Feedback was received from each academic and modifications were made appropriately. In the second phase, the modified online questionnaire was administered to twenty-five experienced senior oil and gas practitioners. The purpose of the pilot study was to assess the clarity of questions and suitability of the respondents and ensure key productivity variables were identified and integrated. The design of the questionnaire was conducted with due attention to the areas of questionnaire focus, phraseology, sequence and overall presentation. The respondents comprised of project directors, project managers, project planners, energy engineers, drilling engineers, geochemists, mining engineers, petroleum engineers and supply chain managers. The selection of these respondents provided a representation of the major parts of the oil and gas industry value chain. It also enabled the validation, accommodation of complementary viewpoints and modification of potential biases of individual respondents. To ensure the appropriate number of completes was achieved, the margin error was set at 5 % and confidence level at 95 %. A total of 500 online questionnaires were distributed to respondents in the UK, the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and South America; 178 responses were received and analysed as per below.
A structural equation modelling was undertaken to simultaneously assess a number of regression equations related to the application of GAI and ML in the oil and gas value chain. Preceding the SEM analysis was a reduction of the number of variables in each of the three categories that were assessed as focal areas where the application of the GAI and ML have influenced the operations in the oil and gas sector. To achieve this, a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was undertaken to explore the variables that significantly explained the tested variables. According to
Choubey and Karmakar [[46]](#page-13-0), PCA is a method for pre-processing high-dimensional data to reduce their dimensions, making it easier to examine using modelling techniques.

#### *3.3.* *Structural equation modelling (SEM) analysis*
An SEM analysis was undertaken using the SPSS AMOS module. SEM analysis is premised on several assumptions considered during this statistical analysis. Kelloway [[47]](#page-13-0) contends that structural equation modelling (SEM) is a flexible yet detailed extension of the general linear model analysis. Bentler and Chou [[48]](#page-13-0) observed that these assumptions ought to be assured or at least approximated in case the outcome of the analysis is to be reliable and valid as well. The assumption of the sample size is cardinal in the SEM analysis. Loehlin [[49]](#page-13-0) proposed that a sample size of 15 cases for every predictor is preferable for the standard OLS multiple regression. This proposal for SEM analysis has been ratified for the SEM analysis as well as a reasonable assumption. Bentler and Chou [[48]](#page-13-0), however, in the assessment of the framing of parameters useable in SEM analysis, disclosed that the researchers intending to undertake an SEM analysis can consider cases as low as five for every parameter estimate. This is, however, advised if the dataset is normally distributed and that outliers or missing cases do not exist.
A careful observation of the discussions of Barrett [[50](#page-13-0)] revealed that they mention five cases per parameter estimate instead of every measured variable. Notably, Streiner [[51]](#page-13-0) admits that the measured variables conventionally have at least a single path coefficient correlated with another variable in the SEM analysis, in addition, a residual term or variance approximation is included therein. What this means, in consideration of the discussions of Bentler and Chou (2016) is that the SEM analysis ought to be 15 cases minimum for every measured variable. From a more generic viewpoint, though, Loehlin [[49](#page-13-0)], while reporting the outcome of a Monte Carlo simulation study through the application of a confirmatory factor analysis model, concluded that investigators need to plan to collect at least 100 entries in the research. The validity of the statistical analysis is in doubt if the smaller sample sizes are used. Barrett [[50]](#page-13-0) for instance, quotes the convergence failures as well as negative error variance estimated for the variables that have been measured in the research. Smaller sample sizes in the SEM analysis equally come with a significantly lowered accuracy level for the parameters. Notably, standard errors in SEM analyses can adequately be computed when larger sample sizes are considered. The selected dataset was audited, and all the assumptions were met.
The objective that was considered for the structural equation modelling in the study was to determine the application of GAI and ML in the enhancement of productivity performance in the oil and gas value chain. - ⁃ Productivity performance; - ⁃ GAI and ML strategy from exploration to production sub-variables; and - ⁃ GAI and ML techniques in supporting the oil and gas industry.

#### *3.4.* *Manifest variables*
The measured variables in the dataset were categorical values measured under the three main sub-themes. They were clustered under three key thematic areas as earlier indicated in the PCA model. The first thematic area was the application of GAI and ML techniques in supporting the oil and gas industry with a total of 12 subdomains. Under the first theme, a total of 12 observed variables were measured. However, after the PCA, four variables were selected for the study as the selected variables in the evaluation of the application of GAI and ML in supporting the oil and gas industry. These observed variables, as illustrated in Table 3, are considered to have been normally distributed in line with the disclosure of Barrett [[50]](#page-13-0). The second theme was the application of GAI and ML strategy from exploration to production in the oil and gas industry. Before the PCA, a total of 10 variables (observed) were present (Table 1); however, after the PCA, a total of three observed variables were selected to be used in the SEM analysis as they explained a sizeable portion of the variation with respect to the second thematic area. The third thematic area was the application of GAI and ML in productivity performance. A PCA reduced the number of the observed variables from the original 10 variables to three variables that explain most of the variance. In this regard, 9 observed variables were used in the SEM analysis (see Table 2). The observed variables in the study were affirmed to be normally distributed in line with the disclosures of Hoe [[52]](#page-13-0).
#### *3.4.1.* *Latent variables*
As illustrated in[ Fig. 1,](#page-5-0) the observed variables in the study are connected to form the latent variables. Under the first theme, the latent variable was the first thematic area, which was the application of GAI and ML in the oil and gas sector. The second latent variable was meant to represent the application of GAI and ML in the productivity performance of oil and gas operations. The third latent variable was the application of GAI and ML strategy from exploration to production. As already indicated, the latent variables in the study conformed to the key assumption in the SEM analysis in terms of their distribution – they have multivariate normal distributions. It was assumed that there was a linear relationship between the latent variables during the analysis and that no multicollinearity existed.

## 5. Discussion

Various components of GAI and ML models are likely to be applied in diverse zones of oil and gas operations. Moreover, in the recent past, these technological concepts have provided an important application in the management of logging within the wells during drilling as well as the management of the engineering operations in the reservoir [58,59]. ## **6.** **Conclusion**
The global dominance of complex brown and greenfield reserves underscores the relevance of contemporary operational approaches and business models in the exploration and production of energy. Such approaches still need to be able to guarantee appropriate profitability for oil and gas production; thus, the present study was designed to assess how GAI and ML can be used to leverage productivity performance in the oil-gas value chain. As established from the reviewed literature, achieving operational effectiveness and productivity performance are crucial for players in the oil and gas industry to remain profitable and maintain high customer satisfaction. As demonstrated in this study, the
application of GAI and ML in the oil and gas sector is designed to revolutionise the oil and gas supply chain by reshaping industry competition, optimising production forecasting across numerous assets, and improving the operational efficiency and output of oil fields. The findings of the study indicate that the application of GAI and ML models will continue to provide an important avenue for mitigating risks in oil and gas operations, lower operational costs therein, resolving emergent issues and automation of data-rich processes.
As illustrated in this study, GAI and ML algorithms will play a significant role in reservoir characterisation and modelling. This will allow oil and gas operators to be able to analyse vast amounts of data, including seismic data and production data. Through the application of GAI and ML algorithms, oil and gas operators will be able to forecast reservoir behaviour, estimate reserves and optimise production strategies. GAI and ML algorithms can also be used to predict equipment failures before they occur. This permits reduced maintenance costs, scheduling, reduced downtime and safety by averting unexpected equipment failures. Moreover, as indicated in this study GAI and ML algorithms can be used to analyse enormous geological and geophysical data. This will permit oil and gas operators to be able to identify patterns and trends that may indicate the presence of oil and gas deposits, allowing operators to make well-versed decisions about where to drill and how to assign their exploration costs. GAI and ML will also play a vital role in augmenting safety and risk management processes, allowing operators to identify potential hazards, assess risks and advance more effective approaches for mitigating risks. By appraising production data and categorising areas of inefficiency, operators can use GAI and ML algorithms to optimise their processes, minimise their consumption of energy and raw materials and reduce waste generation. As generative GAI and ML algorithms advance, their application by oil and gas stakeholders for analysing complex data sets in exploration will become more prevalent. Specifically, in the downstream sector, GAI and ML algorithms can be employed to optimise each phase of the production process, leading to increased output, reduced waste, and enhanced profitability.
## *6.1.* *Theoretical contributions, empirical implications, future research * *directions and limitations*
The findings of the study have several implications for future practice. To ensure the extraction of value from decades of data to perform prescriptive maintenance and optimisation of asset performance. Work will need to be done to establish how GAI and ML algorithms can power oil and gas asset management. As demonstrated in this study, the application of GAI and ML algorithms goes beyond creating efficient processes. We have demonstrated that the GAI and ML algorithms have the potential to leverage productivity and achieve capital effectiveness across the value chain; from initial exploration activities to the end user. Some research themes were not appraised in this study but have been identified as themes for further research. These themes have been outlined as specific for further research. It is imperative to investigate the development of integrated GAI and ML applications that are resilient to fluctuations in oil price. How Digital Twins models can operationally be used to predict, diagnose and forecast asset performance degradation. Although there has been significant research in the application of AI and ML, there is still a need to ascertain how GAI and ML algorithms can be used to scale and extract valid real-time data, especially from a discovery and development viewpoint. Moreover, more research is needed to assess the impact of GA1 and ML with robotics and automation on safety, operational efficiency, and maintenance optimisation. In addition, there is a need to examine how other digital technologies beyond GAI and ML can be used to improve forecasting capabilities in oil and gas exploration; that is, how these technologies can be used to provide more accurate predictions of reservoir behaviour, production rates and equipment performance. This will enable better decision-making, optimise field development strategies and maximise production efficiency.
Beyond the core operational considerations, future studies need to develop frameworks to address ethical concerns and cybersecurity risks associated with AI and ML in the energy sector would ensure more secure and responsible deployment of these technologies. By addressing these gaps and exploring these future directions, subsequent research can build a more comprehensive understanding of how AI and ML can potentially revolutionise the oil and gas sector and drive competitive advantage and innovation.

Edward is a Professor and Head of Project Management programmes at the British University in Dubai. His research interests primarily focus on major project management. He has extensive experience and knowledge of organisational challenges and solution development for managing large capital and heavy engineering projects. He has edited 33 book chapters, published 4 books, 34 book chapters and over 120 refereed papers in refereed journals and conferences. He has supervised 21 PhD students to successful completion and over 300 MSc/MBA industrial projects by research. Edward is currently supervising 10 PhD students. He has also acted as an internal and external examiner of more than 20 PhD students in UK, Australian, United Arab Emirates, Thailand and Malaysian universities. He has secured an estimated £1,064, 700 from a range of funders for several projects and consultancy in project management.
Diana is a Lecturer at Strathmore Business School. She holds a PhD in Business and Management from Strathmore University. Her research predominantly focuses on stakeholder management, value creation and optimisation of information technology projects. Her research interests include appraisal of mega projects, mega project complexity, and stakeholder integration, optimisation of ICT projects, multi-partner collaboration and project-based organisational development. She has been involved in various scholarly research activities, including publications and conference presentations. Further recognition of her research achievements is evident in the several papers she has presented at international conferences, such as the European Academy of Management, British Academy of Management and Project Management Congress, where she shared her knowledge on stakeholder integration, project complexity, delivery and operational effectiveness of projects.
